desc:
citations lists the citation counts of a researcher's papers in non-decreasing order. The h-index is the largest integer h such that at least h papers have h or more citations each (h = 0 is always allowed).

Return the h-index in logarithmic time. For example, [0, 1, 3, 5, 6] gives 3 (the papers with 3, 5 and 6 citations), and [1, 2, 100] gives 2.
constraints: citations is sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: A linear scan over the sorted array works. Because the array is sorted you can do much better; first work out what the condition for a given h looks like in terms of one array cell.
If exactly h papers are to qualify, they are the last h ones, so h is valid exactly when citations[n - h] ≥ h (and h = 0 is always valid). Is validity monotone in h?
Yes: if h is valid, so is h - 1. Binary search the largest h in [0, n] with h == 0 or citations[n - h] ≥ h.
editorial: Let n be the length. For a candidate h, the best choice of papers is the h most cited ones, i.e. citations[n-h .. n-1], and since the array is sorted the weakest of them is citations[n - h]. So h is valid iff citations[n - h] ≥ h.

As h grows, the index n - h moves left (a smaller value) while the required threshold h grows, so once the test fails it fails for every larger h. That makes it a classic last-true search on h in [0, n], taking O(log n) time. Equivalently, you can find the first index i with citations[i] ≥ n - i and return n - i (or 0 if there is none).
